Really disappointing. The infinite spaces get old fast, especially compared to the player's movement speed; there isn't just one extremely large room you need to cross multiple times, it's a consistent feature. The puzzles are extremely simple, with the final puzzles of the game being functionally the same as the first few puzzles, just with the puzzle elements arranged differently. The "alternate route" has some more creativity with the puzzles, but it also involves a lot of finding hidden passages in these gigantic repeating rooms, which is the most frustrating yet boring activity this game has to offer.

The most comparable game I can think of is Antichamber, which also plays with non-euclidean space, except it also has far more puzzle mechanics, far more creativity in the puzzle design, and while very minor, it even opts to present themes/tones conveyed via signposting. Manifold Garden has an ultimate achievement titled "What does it all mean?" which is, frankly, kind of pretentious. It doesn't "mean" anything, it's just some big spaces and a trippy ending sequence.

关卡设计仅仅算中规中矩，但是无限循环的空间足以撑起整个游戏的体验。
玩的时候想到博尔赫斯的《永生》：“在凡夫俗子中间，一切都有无法挽回、覆水难收的意味。”对于拥有无限时间的永生者，一切错过的事情都会发生，甚至发生过的事情也会再次循环。
而当无限的维度变成了空间，传统游戏的空间语法则迎来了彻底的重写。从超级玛丽的时期起，在安全平台上坠落意味着失误与死亡；而在《无限宫苑》的世界里，从安全平台上坠落是游戏体验的必要部分：你会在一段时间的坠落后回到同一个无限重复的平台上，并且你在坠落途中的一切所见都会加深你对世界的理解。

Trippy Portal basically but you use gravity around impossible architecture, where gravity is a tool you redirect at will and the world loops back on itself infinitely in every direction. The visual language it uses pulls from Escher in obvious ways but the actual experience of playing it feels more like being inside a mathematical proof than looking at one.

The puzzles are genuinely challenging. If you come in expecting something in the range of Portal you will probably find this harder, not because the mechanics are more complicated but because the spatial reasoning required operates on a different level. There's no companion to walk you through the logic, no dialogue, no handholding. You figure it out or you sit with it until something clicks, and when it does click the satisfaction is real.

The color design deserves its own mention. Each section of the game operates in a distinct palette and the way color ties into the puzzle mechanics is clever without being obtuse. It's one of the cleaner examples of a game using aesthetics as a functional part of the design rather than just dressing.

The lack of any real story is the honest tradeoff here. There are atmospheric hints at something larger but nothing that resolves into a narrative worth following. If you need a reason beyond the puzzles themselves to keep going, the game doesn't provide one, and that's a legitimate reason some people won't connect with it.

For the right kind of player though, specifically someone who wants a puzzle game that takes its concept seriously and trusts you to meet it halfway, this is worth your time. Just don't go in expecting to revisit it. It's a game you experience once and carry with you.

I've played this game for a lot longer than four hours. Because I’ve mostly been playing in offline mode, Steam hasn’t counted the 18 hours shown by the in-game counter.

And that may be the best indicator of whether Manifold Garden is any good: I kept coming back to it.

It definitely is good - if, and only if, you’re prepared to stick with it.

Unfortunately, Manifold Garden isn’t especially welcoming to new players. Most of the puzzles aren’t that difficult compared with something like The Witness. What makes it difficult, and sometimes frustrating, is the developer’s reluctance to give the player even a small amount of guidance about what they’re supposed to be doing.

Later in the game, you start to get a feel for how its puzzles tend to work. I’m near the end now, and many of the puzzles are variations on things you’ve already seen, but on a much bigger scale.

If you can get through the initial confusion and stick with it, Manifold Garden becomes rather lovely. You get plenty of those satisfying “aha” moments as you work out how a particular mechanism is meant to function - the same kind of feeling you get from games like The Witness or The Talos Principle.

If you enjoy those games, and you’re prepared to persevere through the early stages, Manifold Garden is well worth buying.

Unfortunately, I can't recomment Manifold Garden. While the visuals are quite impressively trippy, it's just... not a very good game. You'll get just about as much enjoyment out of watching someone else play it - and arguably more so. Here's what I mean:

First and foremost, the game is poor from a technical perspective. There are multiple places where the player can soft-lock themselves (I did it twice, once it corrupted my entire save file). This is absolutely inexcusable in a modern title. Difficulty is one thing. Putting the player in a broken state is quite another. I've also managed to get stuck inside geometry in a few places - and no, I wasn't trying to break the game. I would just fall from on high and get jammed in a narrow space where collision with surfaces doesn't work.

Secondly, it's a pretty poor puzzle game. The game's mechanics are fairly simple - looping environment, changing gravity, movable cubes. Each of those feels clunky and underkooed, however. Changing gravity works about half the time, as the game sometimes just refuses to detect surfaces to latch to. There's no mechanic for changing gravity across a convex ledge, meaning the player has to fall over the side and quickly tap to switch gravity to the ledge's surface while in the air. With poor collision detection and strong gravity, this has a high chance of not working. The movable cubes snap to each other but nothing else, leading to several puzzles involving inching forward and placing a cube multiple times to get it "just right". This game would have benefited from a world grid.

The puzzles themselves are... OK. They're decently clever, albeit very simplistic. For the most part, solving a puzzle doesn't require... you know, puzzle-solving. More often than not, it involves slowly traversing large open environments trying to find the requiriste interactive elements, then trying to nail annoying jumps/drops to get cubes where they need to go. Fith very few exceptions, the actual puzzles are paint-by-numbers. It's more a question of figuring out exactly which way the developer wants you to solve them, and which of the interactive elements are entirely superfluous.

My personal breaking point came towards the end, solving a puzzle which involved moving large blokcs by shifting gravity around them, where easily 90% of my time was spent climbing and reclimbing the same flight of stairs just to get back up to the cube tree, over and over again. Almost everywhere else in the game, the terrain would loop in all directions. Not here. Terrain didn't loop top-to-bottom, which is the only direction which mattered as swapping to anything else would move the blocks around and un-solve the puzzle. And this isn't a one-off. Plenty of puzzles are pretty simple once you know the mechanics, but take far longer than they should due to so much padding of walking around and slowly carrying cubes.

And that's when the game even bothers to have puzzles. Much of the time, the player is simply traversing linear paths with next to no interaction. At best, there might be a button to push which opens a door immediately next to it, but there are long stretches of just holding forward - walking long hallways, climbing long staircases, navigating snaking corridors. The visuals are trippy, sure, but that only goes so far and the game doesn't really do much with them anyway. Remember that moment from the trailer where the player emerges into a gigantic series of descending platforms and staircases as far as the eye can see? Yeah, that happens exactly once. Most of the time, the horizon is a blank white void with only sparse floating structures, pretty much none of them explorable.

At the end of the day, I see Manifold Garden as a lesser Antichamber. Both games have similar trippy visuals, both involve figuring out mechanics with very little narrative, but at least Antichamber has decent puzzles which actually capitalise on the weirdness. Manifold Garden, by contrast, has one trick that it uses throughout the entire game. I am very unimpressed.
